items.title: Blue Dragon And 8 Other Completely Unhinged RPG Battle Themes You Need To Listen To
items.summary: I have been informed of the battle theme to Blue Dragon and I have several questions
items.content:
Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 Earthbound Music RPG

Earlier today, my partner came into the room and asked if I’d ever be interested in playing the 2007 Xbox 360 RPG Blue Dragon . This was sort of a weird question, even in our very gaming-centric household, but apparently the reason he asked is that the game is getting an unofficial PC port (as spotted by VGC ).

That’s cool! It’s great that it won’t be stuck on the Xbox 360 anymore and will be accessible to more people. I politely declined to play Blue Dragon at this time (I am busy), but later today the game must have still been on his mind, because my partner sent me this:

That is, I kid you not, apparently the regular-ass battle music in Blue Dragon , a game composed by…Nobuo Uematsu? The Final Fantasy guy?!

Oh my God. This is great. You get like three measures of whatever guitar and then this guy just starts wailing out of tune. And it has lyrics that invoke a ridiculous anime OP from the 90s or something. All while rocking out as hard as possible so that you never lose the momentum of battle. Hell yeah!

I love RPGs, and I love an RPG that’s not afraid to do stuff with its music that’s unconventional. A boss theme that’s calm and soothing rather than intense, a field theme that’s unexpectedly sad, lyrics, rare or specialized instruments, I love it all.

It’s Friday, so in the spirit of Blue Dragon , let’s celebrate its arrival on PC by listening to some other totally unhinged, wacky, or out there regular RPG battle themes together. I will try to stick to regular battle themes, ones for normal ol’ enemies, because if I busted out the boss battles, we’d be here all day.

Let’s start with an oldie but goodie: Pepper Steak (or, if you run with the typo, Peper Steak). Oh, sorry, you think this one is disturbing? Yeah, it’s meant to be. OFF is an RPG about a baseball player “purifying” a messed-up world of blood and meat and plastic by murdering all the ghosts who live in it. Yes, really. Pepper Steak is probably its most infamous theme, with its weird, haunting swing and frequent dissonance and irregular rhythms. Alias Conrad Coldwood, the composer, was unable to return for the 2025 remake, so Toby Fox and Camelia stepped in to make themes for each different zone instead of one overarching Pepper Steak replacement. I have not a single bad word to say about anything Fox has ever composed, but I do think (and he seemed to agree in his statement about it) that it was always going to be impossible to replace Pepper Steak.

I haven’t personally played Shadow Hearts , but I guess this battle theme plays when you go to Japan? Anyway, someone has tried to explain the plot of this game to me a few times, and it hasn’t stuck, but dang if this isn’t an absolutely bonkers thing to have as your regular, normal battle theme for regular, normal enemies for a good chunk of the game.

Nintendo, when are you putting this on the Nintendo music app? This is just workout music. Which I guess is, like, appropriate for the game. But you didn’t have to go this hard.

I don’t need to explain why this is in here, right? This is just Johnny B. Goode by Chuck Berry . The Mother games are all music licensing hell, and I strongly suspect that similar issues in Mother 3 are why we’ll never get an official Western localization. I cannot believe they just put this classic into Earthbound and attached it to the hippie battles. Wild choice.

I strongly felt that something from The World Ends With You belonged on this list due to the series’ daring commitment, on the Nintendo DS of all things, to make its entire soundtrack a straight-up rock and pop album. I was having trouble deciding which theme to go with, though, because while they’re all good, none of them really strike me as the level of off-the-charts wild that the Blue Dragon theme does.

Then I remembered that Transformation, Minamimoto’s absolutely fantastic boss theme, enters the regular battle song rotation in Week 3. Let’s GO. (The remix in NEO is pretty great, too!)

I want to take us briefly in another direction with this list, away from the hard, intense rock songs, and ask you all: what business does this have being a battle theme? This is a song for a minigame in Mario Party , or some pleasant phone hold music. I always find myself bouncing up and down a little while it’s playing. This is another one with a pretty great remix version in the remake. If you want a bonus second theme along these same lines of upbeat minigame music, enjoy Kiss of Jealousy from Live A Live , and from the remake of that too!

items.title: New Tides of Annihilation lead "deeply honored" to take over from Clair Obscur: Expedition 33's Jennifer English, who was "generous, kind, and supportive throughout this whole journey"
items.summary: Gwen is the kind of character that I really love
items.content:
"Gwen is the kind of character that I really love"

In an Instagram reel, Sant'Albano says, "I am so incredibly excited and deeply, deeply honored to finally officially announce that I will be stepping into the role of Gwendolyn in Tides of Annihilation." While many had figured out the Resident Evil Requiem star had taken over after Baldur's Gate 3 and Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 star Jennifer English previously stepped away from the role earlier this year, it was officially confirmed at Gamescom Opening Night Live .

A post shared by Angela Sant’Albano (@angelasantalbano)

"Gwen is the kind of character that I really love," Sant'Albano adds, explaining, "she's full of self-doubt, constantly questions whether she's good enough, but she doesn't let that make her stand still in fear," which somewhat echoes Grace Ashcroft, the Resident Evil role which Sant'Albano is no doubt going to take home countless best performance awards for later this year.

Sant'Albano also mentions English, saying, "Thank you for being so generous, kind, and supportive throughout this whole journey." When she stepped away from the game, it was confirmed that English would stay on the project in an advisory role. Sant'Albano adds in the caption, "I'm honored to carry Gwen's story forward."

Tides of Annihilation still doesn't have a release date, so it'll be a while yet before we get to see Sant'Albano's performance in full, but based on her work and Resident Evil and the latest trailer, I think it's in good hands.

items.title: Clair Obscur Expedition 33: Small Team, Massive Game Clip #1
Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 takes Game of the Year, four other honors at D.I.C.E. Awards
'It's Incredibly Well-Made, But…' — Former PlayStation Boss Warned Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 Devs It Would Be 'Overlooked' if They Called It a Turn-Based RPG
items.summary: Former PlayStation lead Shuhei Yoshida warned the developers behind Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 about calling it a "turn-based RPG" because "that alone might cause players to overlook it.
items.content:
Former PlayStation lead Shuhei Yoshida warned the developers behind Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 about calling it a "turn-based RPG" because "that alone might cause players to overlook it."

Yoshida, who served as PlayStation's head of indies and president of Sony Interactive Entertainment Worldwide Studios before stepping down in 2024, spoke about some key advice he gave the award-winning team during a recent lecture for indie game developers. Portions of that lecture were then reported by 4Gamer and subsequently translated by Automaton , including one piece of advice he gave to publisher Kepler Interactive while advising the team ahead of its April 2025 launch.

"It’s incredibly well-made, but it would be better not to call it a turn-based RPG," Yoshida warned the Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 devs. "That alone might cause players to overlook it."

But why? Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 went on to receive praise from fans and critics (including a 9/10 review from IGN), while ending its already explosive year with big wins across The Game Awards , BAFTA , DICE , and IGN award shows. Its positive reception was so intense that even the developers at Sandfall Interactive weren't prepared for its towering Metacritic score .

Yoshida acknowledged Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 as a quality release long before it reached the hands of the public. He was impressed early on, calling attention to its "combination of turn-based JRPG mechanics and real-time action inputs reminiscent of The Legend of Dragoon." The problem, however, was that, at the time, he was concerned its success could be affected by what he observed to be a tendency for turn-based JRPGs to be seen as outdated.

Game-award-winning formula or not, Yoshida feared Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 would be ignored by some gamers if they saw that "turn-based" label. As a result, Kepler got creative and instead started selling Sandfall's first game as an experience with "reactive turn-based battles" instead, and the rest is history.

The game, of course, went on to become a massive sales success despite its proximity to the launch of The Elder Scrolls 4: Oblivion . Yoshida said he's since noticed an uptick in reports from publishers receiving pitches for new turn-based RPGs.

While we wait to see what's next from Yoshida and Sandfall, you can see why the developers behind Final Fantasy Resonance think turn-based RPGs are making a huge comeback . You can also read the devs' conversation about canon endings and the writer who got their start at Sandfall .

Michael Cripe is a freelance writer with IGN. He's best known for his work at sites like The Pitch, The Escapist, and OnlySP. Be sure to give him a follow on Bluesky (@mikecripe.bsky.social) and Twitter (@MikeCripe).

items.title: The Switch 2 is already starting to show its seams
items.summary: Clair Obscur's status on the console reveals the truth
items.content:
on Google Preferred Source Google News Link copied to clipboard By Giovanni Colantonio Published Aug 1, 2026, 9:00 AM EDT Switchboard Getting big games running on Nintendo's console is no easy task

Image: Sandfall interactive/Kepler Interactive Sign in to your Polygon.com account Add Us Add on Google Preferred Source Google News Summary Generate a summary of this story Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Thread 41 Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap Switchboard is Polygon's weekly newsletter for all things Nintendo, sent on Thursdays and published on the site on Saturdays. You can subscribe here .

Just one year into the Switch 2’s lifespan, Nintendo’s console feels like a technical miracle. It’s downright shocking that it can run modern games like Resident Evil Requiem and Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth with minimal compromises, or that new games like Onimusha: Way of the Sword will launch on it at the same time as on PS5 and Xbox Series X. For Nintendo fans who spent decades pining for third-party games that never came to underpowered machines like the Wii, it feels like the Switch 2 can do it all. Except it can’t.

We got a reality check this week courtesy of Sandfall Interactive, the developer of last year’s Game of the Year winning Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 . In a new interview with Automaton Media , Sandfall co-founder Tom Guillermin explained that the team wants to bring its hit RPG to Switch 2, but said that it would be a “big technical challenge” to pull off.

The problem? Unreal Engine 5. Clair Obscur heavily relied on the engine’s features to make its game, especially taking advantage of Blueprints (a scripting tool that lets developers plug nodes together to craft gameplay systems). The team said that many of those features simply don’t work on Switch 2 at present. “They’re introducing features like Lumen Lite now, which is easier to run than the standard Lumen,” lead character and concept artist Alan Reynaud explained, “but these things take time to roll out, so we’ll have to consider the updates coming from Unreal Engine to determine what to do.” With some Switch 2 ports, developers are simply at the mercy of Epic for now.

This isn’t the first example of a developer struggling to get its game working on Switch 2. Last year, 2K Games indefinitely delayed the Switch 2 release of Borderlands 4 for “additional development and polish time.” Closing in on one year later, we haven’t heard a peep about it since. (Though Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick told Game File that the project hadn't been cancelled earlier this year.)

Image: FromSoftware/Bandai Namco Then there’s the long-running saga of Elden Ring: Tarnished Edition . First announced during the Switch 2’s full reveal Direct with a 2025 release window, the port faced a year-long delay after hands-on impressions out of last year’s Gamescom raised some serious red flags. Finally set to release on Aug. 28, Elden Ring will now land as a crucial stress test for Switch 2. FromSoftware’s ability to get the open-world game — one that was released on PS4 and Xbox One — running well on the hardware will tell us a lot about how flexible Nintendo’s dream machine is. (The good news is that it seems to be in much better shape than it was last year.)

The reality is that the Switch 2 still has its limits, even though companies like Capcom and Square Enix have seemingly cracked the console’s code. It takes hard work to get Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth running on the hardware, and that’s a challenge for smaller teams like Sandfall Interactive who may not have the resources to invest in time-consuming ports. We’re still far off from a reality where every third-party game will get a Switch 2 version, and that will only become apparent if a new console generation begins midway through the Switch 2’s lifespan.

Never forget that The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild felt like a miracle when fans first played it on the go in 2017. Eight years later, Switch owners were begging for an upgrade. That’s the nature of hardware, and the Switch 2 will not be immune to that cycle in the long run.

The formerly VR-exclusive Moss series made its way to consoles this month, and it feels right at home on Switch. The pair of games featured in Moss: The Forgotten Relic are both delightful, kind-hearted adventures starring an adorable mouse. (The pint-sized hero melted Austin Manchester’s heart, as you can read in his review .) It doesn’t get much more Nintendo than that.

A classic arcade series makes its return this week with Truxton Extreme , so it’s a good weekend to pay some respects to Truxton creator Toplan, the master of the shoot-’em-up genre. The best way to do that is by jumping into one of its most iconic games, Mega Drive classic Zero Wing . Yes, it’s the game that gave us “All your base are belong to us,” but it’s also a tense sci-fi shump with a killer soundtrack to boot.

It feels like summer just began, but we’ve already reached August. Don’t let the last few weeks of heat slip away; toss on the Wave Race 64 soundtrack today. It’s full of sunny beachside anthems, including this radical prog rock jam that feels like it was plucked right out of an 80s movie. (There's a playlist of all of Switchboard's music picks here .)

Xenoblade Chronicles 2 — Nintendo Switch 2 Edition

items.title: "It's a sad decision." Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 developers on the end of physical disc production and why they pushed for a physical release despite the drawbacks
items.summary: Interview with Sandfall Interactive's core members about what physical games mean to them.
items.content:
Home Interviews “It’s a sad decision.” Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 developers on the end of physical disc production and why they pushed for a physical release despite the drawbacks Interview with Sandfall Interactive's core members about what physical games mean to them.

Interviews 2026-07-29 00:01 Genki 4 Epic Games Japan and Sandfall Interactive recently hosted a Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 postmortem event in Yokohama, Japan, where the developers shared technical insights into the making of 2025’s Game of the Year. Following the event, AUTOMATON sat down with the team and took the opportunity to ask about their thoughts on physical game releases. With PlayStation set to end game disc production in 2028, the developers briefly reflected on why they insisted on releasing Expedition 33 physically despite the added challenges, and discussed why they believe physical editions remain important to video games as a medium.

Guillaume Broche – Sandfall Interactive CEO and Creative Director Tom Guillermin – Sandfall Interactive Co-founder and CTO Alan Reynaud – Lead Character and Concept Artist Alexandre Breton – Technical Artist

For more about Sandfall Interactive’s Japanese influences, thoughts on Unreal Engine, and studio upsizing, check out part one of this interview .

— PlayStation recently announced that it will end physical disk production in 2028. What are your thoughts on that?

Guillaume Broche: Personally, I find it super sad because I really like video game stores. And even if nowadays, I play mainly on PC myself, we have a lot of people on the team who play on PS5 and love to collect physical discs. I think it’s part of the beauty of art too – that it’s something tangible that you can touch. I completely appreciate that people want to have their rows of DVDs and games and just feel that they own them. So I think it’s a shame. I mean, business-wise, I can understand why it may make sense, but I think in terms of the artistry of video games, it’s a sad decision.

Tom Guillermin: In our discussions with our publisher prior to the release of Expedition 33, the question of whether or not to do a physical release cropped up. A physical release adds more constraints because you have to account for the production time of the physical items, and you also earn less money per copy.

But for us, physical was something special. We also felt that the game could be special to players, and that they would want to, as Guillaume said, hold it in their hands.

So even though it made things harder and meant less money per unit, it was important for us to provide players who want to have the physical game in their hands with an option. Because that’s what we value as players too.

Guillaume Broche: To add to that, there were two very strong moments when the game released. After launch, we went to a video game store to buy our own game (laughs). Just as a gesture. And another strong memory I have is when someone from Japan sent me a picture [of our game] from a video game store – in Akihabara I think – in Japanese writing and all. I felt like a kid when I saw it. I was like “Yeah, it’s real!” It starts feeling real when you see it in stores. Alan Reynaud: Even now when I’m going to the supermarket or something, if I see our game in a store, it always makes my day. It’s a bit selfish, because it’s our game, but it always makes me go “Oh!”

Knowing that may not be possible again makes me a bit sad. And maybe it’s the child in me, but I like to go outside, buy a game, and come back home with it. It’s a nice feeling.

Alexandre Breton: And it’s not just because it’s “our game.” I think what’s cool [about physical games in general] is that a few years later, you’ll have your box, and you can hold it and look at the title and remember all the memories that are linked to the game.

Alan Reynaud: I think the same principle can apply to manga. It’s nice to read on your phone and stuff, but having a real book is just a different feeling. And I don’t think we could imagine a world where manga is just scanned and stored on your computer. It would be sad to not have it in your library. I think the same applies for games. Sure, it makes more sense business-wise, but you lose the spirit of it.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is available for PC ( Steam ), PS5 and Xbox Series X|S.

items.title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 & the Beauty of a Non-Definitive Ending
items.summary: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 gives Maelle and Verso two painful endings. This feature examines grief, escapism, and why neither choice is wrong.
items.content:
Imagine: it’s PAX West 2025, and you’re me, wandering the expo hall with hundreds if not thousands of others. It’s a sea of people, but amongst them, you start to notice an incredibly peculiar pattern: dotting the crowd are bright red French berets. You cross direct paths with someone and notice their red beret is not only accompanied by a black-and-white striped shirt, but a red checked sash, strapping a fake plastic baguette to their back. You’re immediately both intrigued and perplexed, and raise the obvious question to your partner, who explains it’s from that game he started playing “with Charlie Cox in it”.

In this scenario, you are very much a fan of Charlie Cox and his starring in Daredevil, so you’re immediately reminded of what he’s talking about in that explanation – Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. You vaguely remember seeing the first casting announcement trailer for it during a random State of Play one early morning and getting excited because Daredevil(!), but ultimately you ended up going back to your endless, hellish cycle of Marvel Rivals lobbies when the game actually released. The red berets are a kind reminder of your previous excitement about the game, though, and it isn’t long after that you find yourself glued to your television while being serenaded by a beautiful French accent as you are formally introduced to the citizens of Lumiere. Your four years of French classes throughout school surely prepared you for this moment.

What you aren’t prepared for is just how much of an effect this game has on you by the end.

Now, at the risk of being honest, it’s a complete understatement to say I love this game. If you have interacted with me within the last year, I have talked to you about this game, or I have told you to finish it after you told me you didn’t even get through Act I, or I have endlessly gushed over Lorien Testard’s soundtrack what was probably an annoying amount. It’s rare to find yourself so committed to a piece of media, if only because you see yourself reflected in it so wholly, whether it’s in Maelle’s escapism or Verso’s self-sacrificial tendencies. After all, you don’t win 37 awards because people just feel pretty okay emotions about your game. As is with any piece of media, though, comes what others have to say about it.

(Obligatory note: What’s discussed going forward is riding off of the notion that the person reading this has played the game. If you haven’t, maybe go open Steam or the PlayStation store, grab some tissues, strap in for a bit, and hopefully you will thank me later. Or feel free to keep reading – I’m certainly not stopping you).

One of the gaming community’s most divisive conversations regarding Expedition 33 is regarding the two distinct endings the game has to offer, notwithstanding how both are unique in how they highlight the game’s central theme around the idea of grief. There hasn’t been a day that’s gone by in recent memory where I haven’t been faced with someone explaining how “[insert your preferred character’s name] ending is the right one”, or “if you chose [insert your not-preferred character’s name] ending, you’re clearly heartless”.

In the first ending, the audience is brought back to Lumiere after Maelle and Verso’s battle, and we see that Maelle has not erased the canvas, which was her motivation by the end of Act III. We’re rejoined by the ensemble we’ve grown to love, the Expeditioners as well as Esquie and Monoco, and we even see that Gustave and Sophie have both been repainted after their previous deaths. We’re also faced with Maelle and a considerably older Verso. We see Verso struggle for an uncomfortable moment, his hands stretching out and freezing over keys of a grand piano in Lumiere’s opera house, until it can be discerned Maelle uses her Paintress abilities in order to force the painted version of her late brother to play.

The colors are washed. The lighting is dimmed. It doesn’t yield much comfort aside from the embrace of familiar faces, but that just might be enough.

The second ending is an intentionally stark contrast. For the first time in the game, we’re officially brought outside of the canvas now that it’s presumably been destroyed, as that was Verso’s desire by the end game, and we’re shown the Dessendre’s. In front of them sits a grave donning the name “Verso Dessendre”. Renoir and Aline share a tender embrace in front of their son’s grave, Clea leaves behind a bouquet of achingly familiar red and white flowers before excusing herself, and we see a scarred Alicia– or Maelle– standing by as she watches the scene unfold, holding a sewn Esquie doll. The camera turns and we see the images of the very same Expeditioners, including Gustave and Verso’s painted self, framed by the Eiffel Tower as they wave goodbye before dissipating.

The colors are bright. It’s backlit by a sunny day. The comfort is uncertain and bittersweet, but it’s ultimately not an unwelcome feeling, either.

Undeniably, the discussion around these endings is, of course, typically viewed as black-and-white as possible. More often than not, when faced with multiple endings by the end of a game, audiences are used to getting a “good” ending and a “bad” ending, leaving little room for discussion. And, in these cases, that is the game’s intent. In these cases, the games do have a black-and-white, a good-and-bad. It’s not unheard of for a game to punish a player for making poor choices throughout a play through. When looking at Expedition 33’s endings, though, this mindset is frankly doing a disservice to the game’s theming as a whole.

Grief as a theme is interwoven throughout the entire game, and when is the process of grieving ever black-and-white? Grief by all accounts is an incredibly non-linear process. We have all grieved over someone, over something, and we all understand what that means. Both of the endings evoke very different emotions, but it really is up to the player and what they choose to prioritize within their own grief. Yes, in Maelle’s ending, we see the way she chooses to use her Paintress abilities against her brother and father’s wishes, but more importantly, she’s also surrounded by those she has come to love, in a fully-functioning body. She’s given grace to those who have only ever lived inside of the canvas, reasserting the idea that they are sentient individuals with their own lives and autonomy, despite the circumstances they were painted into. Within Verso’s ending, the Dessendre’s are now able to work on moving past their shared grief regarding the loss of their real-life brother and son after years of stagnation, but at the cost of Alicia having a healthy physical body, and at the loss of everyone we have come to love inside of the canvas.

Both of these endings offer a resolution and catharsis in their own ways, and the outcome of one doesn’t make the other more or less right. When discussing these endings, we can’t assume why someone chose one ending over the other, because their grief surrounding the game is ultimately their own, and it’s not up to us to dictate how that feels to them. It can’t be stressed enough how sacrificing nuance in these discussions doesn’t only do a disservice to the game, but also the players and their own emotions about it.

I have a confession to make: I wholeheartedly chose Maelle’s ending the first time I played, and at that moment, it wasn’t a difficult choice for me. It made sense. I had grown so incredibly fond of Lumiere and the canvas and those inside of it, just like Maelle, but I saw myself in so many facets of her. I was a sixteen-year-old girl once, finding escape in worlds I created and in the media I was in love with, be it novels or games or movies, in order to remove myself from the very real grief I was experiencing. It’s something I still find myself doing even in adulthood, and ironically, probably the reason why I found myself so absorbed in Expedition 33 in the first place. The hours I put into the game were the direct result of me needing a distraction from life, and to watch the game slowly begin to unveil what it truly was felt like looking into a mirror. Of course I chose to save Lumiere. Of course I sided with Maelle. It’s what I do all the time. More often than not, I run from my grief rather than let myself feel it, and instead I look for reassurance and acceptance and comfort in worlds where my real feelings can’t hurt me. It’s far easier to feel for the characters on my screen than it is to feel for myself. After all, their emotions aren’t tangible, unlike my own. Expedition 33 was the first time I had ever personally experienced a piece of media that conveyed that feeling in a way that felt so specific, and so undeniably real.

Expeditioners!

Following the huge demand from so many of you, we’ve been working super hard to be able to finally announce that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, is now available with Arabic text!

This brings the total number of supported languages to 20!

With the new Arabic language support, we had to consider additional changes to the game’s UI to ensure a smooth and enjoyable experience for Arabic-speaking players around the world.

Adding Arabic localization has been a true team effort over many months, from the incredible adaptation and localization work carried out by the linguists, to reworking the vast majority of the user interface for right-to-left reading, all the way through localization testing.

Every team involved brought passion and dedication to making this possible, and we couldn’t be more grateful for their work. We hope this update makes the story feel even more personal to our players.

Today’s update also includes some additional fixes and improvements. Read the full patch notes here!

Thank you all so much for your continued support! <3

Tomorrow comes.

~ The Expedition 33 Team

Today marks 1 year since we released Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. This past year has been an incredible journey and so we have a few things to share with you today. 

 

To celebrate the occasion, the team put together a special piece of artwork that we hope you will enjoy! 

8 Million Copies Sold

Thank you so so much to every single person who has played, created art, shared, streamed, discussed, and supported this game!!

Game Update: New Haircuts + Patch Notes

We've pushed a fun little update live today: new haircuts are now available in-game, giving the expedition even more style to strut around in! 💅 

For the full list of changes, fixes, and improvements, you can read the patch notes here

Community Emotes

We commissioned some of our amazing community creators to design official Expedition 33 emotes for you to use in your own channels! 

A massive thank you to IrunoArt, comickergirl (Sarah Leuver), and Bugyakis for their brilliant work on each of these!!

They're FREE to download and use here

Official Baguette Merch

In the mood to add some baguette to your wardrobe? 

We’ve partnered with Orcival and Le Béret Français to bring you the official Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 striped shirt and beret for your cosplays! 🥖    You can purchase the official Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 x Orcival mariniere here

And the official Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 x Le Béret Français beret is available to buy here

On top of that, keep an eye out for a limited number of units of the Monolith Set to be back in stock from our partners at Laced and Pix n' Love soon!! 

And Finally… Cake

It's been a big day for us. Thank you for making it possible. 🎂 

And if you know someone who wants to pick up the game, we're running a 20% sale right now on Steam - As well as some fun merchandise goodies available on our merch page!

Merch Page

From the bottom of our hearts, we’re so thankful to each and every one of you – this has been the best year of our lives, thanks to you. 

 

- The Expedition 33 Team

items.title: Charlie Cox has finally played Clair Obscur: Expedition 33—a bit
items.summary: The star of Stardust and Daredevil previously admitted to not having tried the game he stars in.
items.content:
The star of Stardust and Daredevil previously admitted to not having tried the game he stars in.

Good for him. You don't want to join us down here in the pit, spending the rest of our lives trying to convince people Fallout 2 wasn't as good as the first one. Get out while you still can.

When Charlie Cox admitted he hadn't played Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 , even though he voices Gustave in it, that seemed fair enough to me. It's a 45-hour JRPG with a frankly quite divisive ending. You don't need that in your life while also trying to maintain Daredevil's abs.

In a more recent interview with our comrades at GamesRadar , however, Cox said he finally got around to playing it. A bit. "Not the whole thing," he added. "I haven't completed it." He's seen the impressive introductory area, though. "I've played the opening bit for a while and kind of walked around and met the people and garnered the information and all that kind of stuff. Not very well."

Cox highlighted how different Clair Obscur felt when compared to the videogames he grew up with, like Goldeneye, Mario Kart, and FIFA 98. "They weren't, like, stories that were so carefully carved out and created over the course of a game with the level of detail and the way in which information is received. It's not just all spelled out—you discover these things as you go on through the game," Cox said.

It must be an uncanny experience, playing a videogame as a character you've provided the voice for. "It didn't really feel like me... I didn't really think of it as me, I thought of it as Gustave."

J.K. Simmons hasn't played Baldur's Gate 3 or any of his games, but he loves Portal 2: 'I could have done the feature film, or the play, or whatever' Ray Chase, the voice of Cyclops in X-Men '97, has '1,000 freaking hours' in Slay the Spire and is running a 'smell build' in Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2: ' I wear perfumes and walk into battle with my fancy boy outfit' Clair Obscur is flawed on purpose, says director: 'Games that try to be perfect, that try to fix all their flaws—they're usually just really boring' Though he didn't say whether he'll go back to play more, I suspect Cox won't be collecting all the achievements any time soon. He seemed sensibly incredulous when he said, "there are people who've played it, there are people who've completed it, there are people who have 100%ed it, which—as far as I could work out—is 50-plus hours, maybe 100 hours, sometimes, of gameplay." Honestly, that is too much, and he's right to say it.

items.title: The developers of Clair Obscur gave me an interview and some advice
items.summary: We spoke about the game's finale (don't worry, there are spoiler warnings), the best Pictos, and what I can be doing better.
items.content:
Stephen Totilo Mar 27, 2026 35 3 1 Share Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. Screenshot: Sandfall Interactive, captured by Game File This story, perhaps appropriately, goes on a bit longer than you might expect, past what may feel like the conclusion.

This was not by design. In my business of reporting, you can’t plan surprise endings. But it is what delightfully happened.

This story is merely an accurate account of my absurd endeavor from earlier this month, when I tried to finally play through 2025’s most acclaimed video game, the role-playing phenomenon Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 , in a sudden rush.

I had a deadline: a date when I expected to have a chance to chat about Clair Obscur with some of its creators. We would perhaps discuss the game’s ending, which, in their business of making video games, they could plan for.

I will get to all of that. I will get to Thursday night, March 12, when I spoke to two of Clair Obscur’s creators, discussed the ending and got myself an in-person consultation about my characters’ builds.

It’s Sunday, March 8 and I have downloaded Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 to the portable ROG Xbox Ally X , a Switch-looking device that can run games offered via Xbox Game Pass. At this point, I have only played a little past the prologue of Clair Obscur, back on an Xbox in my house. Cloud saving has transferred my progress to the portable. In the game, our protagonist Gustave and his sort-of sister Maelle have set out on Expedition 33, the latest annual beach landing of adventurers who hope they will be the ones to take down the distant and mysterious paintress, who somehow, magically annihilates everyone of a certain age each year.

I know I’ve given myself barely enough time to play through this game ahead of Thursday, when Clair Obscur is likely to win another pile of awards at the former Game Developers Conference (now GDC Festival of Gaming) and when I’ll be backstage with an opportunity to interview the winners.

In the weeks prior, I’ve been busy writing and reporting and, in terms of actually using a controller, playing through Resident Evils .

Just back in February, I had been backstage at a different gaming awards event, where I’d met some of the makers of Clair Obscur and where I’d not spoken to them about the game, because I had other coverage goals for my chats with the winners.

For the Game Developers Choice Awards on March 12, though, I want to talk about the games. My friend urges me on. You should try to finish Clair Obscur, he says. They haven’t spoken about the ending all that much, yet it’s all the game’s fans talk about. You gotta find out what happens, he says, even if you just have to watch a video. Perish the thought.

So I’m on United Airlines flight 1777 from EWR to SFO, comfortably seated in window seat 39A. My Ally X is in my hands, and Clair Obscur is running, well before takeoff. I’ve boarded fairly early. Soon, a man with long curly hair takes the middle seat next to me. There is still plenty of elbow room for me, and I start playing. Best I can tell, the man in the middle seat soon starts a nap.

Gustave, alongside a magically powered woman named Lune, are fighting enemies called Nevrons in dramatic turn-based fights. They reunite with red-haired Maelle. As the plane takes off and begins to cross the United States, things are going well. I’m loving the combat and the look of the game’s world.

Before my plane lands, I reach the end of Clair Obscur’s first act. Big twist! I’ve been rushing, avoiding sidequests, and, wow. I did not see that coming. I’m stunned, but I don’t think anyone on the flight notices. I make sure not to disturb the curly-haired guy next to me, who I think at this point is watching a movie?

After my flight lands, I text my friend to confirm that I have not seen Clair Obscur’s wildest turn. I have not.

items.title: Death is Always Brutal: Reflections on Clair Obscur Expedition 33
items.summary: Death is always brutal. Death is always violent. There is no glossing over this reality.
items.content:
This article contains potential spoilers for Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 .

We can’t hide from death even though our culture can often be accused of trying to do so. Our dreams of trans-humanism, systematic acceptance of nursing homes, and transition to “celebrations of life” rather than funerals do offer some validity to that claim. However, we can overestimate the effect that any of these trends and tendencies have on obscuring our view of the Reaper and his trusty scythe.

For the simple and obvious fact is that we humans just can’t sweep death under the rug. There is no running from it in the end—and neither can we hide ourselves from it while we live. Naturally then, works of art will deal directly with this fact, no matter how death-shy our culture may seem.

In the spring of 2025, a small French video game company named Sandfall Interactive launched their first game. With its incredible cast of characters, stunning design and artwork, captivating story, and masterful soundtrack, it made quite a splash in the gaming world. It not only won “Game of the Year” at the 2025 Game Awards, but also set a record for most awards won. But perhaps nowhere did it stand out more than in its extended reflection on death and grief, and its willingness to leave players deeply moved and uncomfortable in the end.

Death is always brutal. Death is always violent. There is no glossing over this reality.

The game’s title, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 , points to the duality of its themes. Similar to the Italian term chiaroscuro , the French term clair obscur —which literally translates to “light dark”—refers to works of art that utilize a strong contrast and interplay between light and darkness, creating an emotionally rich and dynamic visual. The light and darkness not only contrast each other, but also complement one another. The light shines brighter and the dark weighs heavier due precisely to the presence of their opposite extremes.

One of the game’s primary themes is grief. Each character of the main protagonist family portrays a different expression of coping with loss. Few of their expressions (if any) are healthy, but they’re all realistic. Midway through the story, one of the protagonists, Maelle, suffers an immense loss and becomes overwhelmed by the death that surrounds her team wherever they go. In a conversation with an immortal character named Verso, she laments death’s omnipresence:

Verso: “Hey, you holding up? We’re almost there.”

Maelle: “Holding up? Everywhere we go, just death, death, and more death. Everywhere we go, just death. I just—I don’t want to see that anymore.”

Maelle: “I thought you would understand. You said you spent your immortality burying the people around you. Doesn’t any of this bother you?”

Maelle knew she would be facing death. Though young, she was anything but naïve. She set out on Expedition 33 to fight deadly enemies (known as nevrons ) in an effort to stop a cycle of death called the Gommage , which kills the world’s oldest citizens each year. With every passing year, the age limit has decreased by one, and now sits at 33.

Each year, the Gommage erases the oldest citizens, who gently dissolve into a wisp of flowers. It’s even celebrated with a festival and flowers, eerily echoing our celebrations of life. Maelle has witnessed this annual killing 16 times (assuming she was an observant infant). In one sense, she is used to death. But now, she is faced with a reality check.

Is she used to it? Can she, or anyone, ever be used to it? Having left the general comfort and safety of her city of Lumière, she is faced with these tough questions. Sure, the effect of death hasn’t changed, but the appearance of death has. As if all this time, the Reaper was wearing a colorful outfit and a friendly mask, only to now reveal himself as he really is: Death unmasked . Maelle discuss this change with her adoptive guardian Gustave:

Maelle: “Death out here’s not like death in Lumière, is it? I—uh, I thought I was used to losing people…But not—not like that—on the beach…that man…”
